title: Drunken Leaders and the Tested Cornerstone
summary: Isaiah pronounces woe on Samaria, the proud crown of Ephraim's drunkards, whose glory will be swallowed like an early fig, and then turns to Jerusalem's priests, prophets, and rulers, who are just as drunk and who mock his plain teaching. They boast of a covenant with death that will protect them, but God will lay in Zion a tested cornerstone, and their refuge of lies will be swept away. A closing parable of the farmer shows that God's judgments, like a farmer's work, are measured and wise.
story: After the sweeping vision of chapters 24 to 27, the book returns to the streets of Samaria and Jerusalem. Chapter 28 opens a new section, chapters 28 to 33, marked by a series of woes (28:1; 29:1, 15; 30:1; 31:1; 33:1) that deal with the Assyrian threat and Judah's temptation to seek safety in alliances, especially with Egypt. The pattern of this chapter will repeat through the section: a sharp warning against false security, a promise of what God himself will provide, and a reminder that his purposes are wiser than human schemes. The foundation stone laid in Zion is one of Isaiah's great promises, and the New Testament will return to it more than once.
historical:
Verses 1 to 4 address Ephraim, the northern kingdom of Israel, whose capital Samaria stood on a hill rising above a fertile valley, like a wreath on a drinker's head. This oracle must come from before 722 BC, when Samaria fell to Assyria after a siege of about three years (2 Kings 17:5-6). The "one who is strong and mighty" of verse 2 is Assyria, used by the LORD as his instrument.

From verse 7 the prophet turns to Jerusalem's leaders, and verse 14 addresses them directly. Their "covenant with death" (verse 15) is most often understood as a political alliance, probably Judah's negotiations with Egypt during Hezekiah's reign. After the Assyrian king Sargon II died in 705 BC, Hezekiah joined other states in revolt against Assyria and looked to Egypt for support, which led to Sennacherib's invasion in 701 BC (chapters 36 and 37). Isaiah calls this alliance an agreement with death, perhaps with a bitter play on Mot, the Canaanite god of death, or on Egyptian concern with the afterlife; some scholars also see a reference to consulting the dead. The historical references in verse 21 look back to David's victories: at Baal-perazim he broke through the Philistines (2 Samuel 5:20), and in 1 Chronicles 14:16 he struck them down from Gibeon to Gezer. Some interpreters instead connect Gibeon with Joshua's battle there (Joshua 10). God once fought for Israel in those places; now his "strange work" will be to fight against his own people.
cultural:
Drinking at feasts and religious festivals was part of ancient life, and a garland of flowers was sometimes worn at banquets. Isaiah's picture of a fading wreath on the head of a drunk describes Samaria's leaders at the end of the party. The priests and prophets of Jerusalem are no better (verses 7 and 8). Their mocking reply in verse 10 is hard to translate. The Hebrew is a string of short syllables, tsav latsav, qav laqav, which may imitate baby talk, the chanting of a child learning letters (tsade and qoph are neighboring letters of the Hebrew alphabet), or the sound of a foreign language. The point is clear either way: they treat Isaiah's message as simple-minded, so God will speak to them in the incomprehensible speech of foreign invaders (verse 11).

The building imagery of verses 16 and 17 comes from ancient construction. A cornerstone was the first and largest stone laid, set carefully in the foundation to fix the lines of the whole building. Builders tested stones for soundness; a measuring line and a plumb line or level checked that walls were straight. The farming parable of verses 23 to 29 reflects real practice: small seeds like caraway and cumin were beaten out with sticks because a threshing sledge would crush them, while heavier grain was threshed by driving carts or animals over it. Different crops were sown in their own places, and some translations name the last crop spelt rather than rye.
literary: The chapter is a set of oracles bound together by the ideas of drunkenness, refuge, and the word of the LORD. It opens with a woe (verse 1), the funeral cry that begins each unit of this section. The image of the crown moves from the fading crown of Samaria (verses 1 to 4) to the LORD himself as a crown of glory for the remnant (verse 5). The scoffers' own words are turned against them twice: the nonsense syllables of verse 10 return as the word of judgment in verse 13, and their boast in verse 15 is answered clause by clause in verses 17 and 18 (hail sweeps away the refuge of lies, the covenant with death is annulled, the scourge tramples them). The closing parable (verses 23 to 29) shifts into the style of wisdom literature, teaching through observation of ordinary life, and ends by calling the LORD "wonderful in counsel," an echo of the royal name in 9:6.

outline.t: Woe to Samaria, the fading crown of drunkards
The LORD a crown of glory for the remnant
Jerusalem's drunken priests and prophets mock the message
The covenant with death and the stone laid in Zion
The parable of the farmer: God's measured wisdom

doctrines.note: Against every false refuge, God lays his own foundation in Zion, and "the one who believes will never be shaken" (verse 16). Faith is not one strategy among many; it is resting on what God has laid down.

God's judgment on his own people is called his "strange work" (verse 21), foreign to his usual purpose of blessing. Yet like a farmer's threshing, it is measured, purposeful, and never endless (verses 27 and 28).

The farmer's skill comes from God, who "instructs and teaches him properly" (verse 26). The chapter ends by grounding ordinary practical wisdom in God, whose counsel is wonderful and whose wisdom excels.

words.note: Bochan, testing. This rare word describes the stone God lays in Zion as a tested or proven stone. It may mean a stone that has passed inspection, or a stone that itself tests those who build on it. Either way, the foundation of Zion's security is something God supplies and guarantees.

Pinnah, corner. The cornerstone set the orientation of the whole building. The word is also used figuratively of leaders, as the cornerstones of a people (Judges 20:2). Psalm 118:22 speaks of the stone the builders rejected becoming the head of the corner, and the New Testament brings these two passages together.

Sheol, the realm of the dead. It is the place where all the dead go in much of the Old Testament, pictured as a deep pit or silent land. Jerusalem's rulers claim to have made an agreement with it, a mocking description of a treaty that promised them safety but would lead to death.

christ: The New Testament quotes verse 16 several times and identifies the stone with Jesus. Paul quotes it in Romans 9:33 and 10:11, following the Greek translation (the Septuagint, made in the last centuries before Christ), which reads that the one who believes will not be put to shame. First Peter 2:4-8 joins it with Psalm 118:22 and Isaiah 8:14 to present Christ as the living stone, chosen and precious to God, rejected by people, and the foundation on which believers are built as a spiritual house. Paul also cites verses 11 and 12 in 1 Corinthians 14:21, where he discusses speaking in tongues. These are not arbitrary uses: Isaiah promised a foundation God himself would lay, and the apostles saw that foundation in the crucified and risen Jesus.

hard.q: What does it mean that judgment is God's "strange work" and "disturbing task"?
hard.a:
Verse 21 recalls places where God fought for Israel against her enemies, then says he will now rise up in the same way against Jerusalem. The work is strange because it seems contrary to his character and his covenant: the God who defended Zion now brings enemies against it. Readers have taken this in two main ways. Some emphasize that judgment is truly alien to God's heart, which delights in mercy (compare Lamentations 3:33 and Ezekiel 18:32). Others emphasize the shock to Judah: the leaders assumed God was on their side no matter what, and the strange work is his refusal to protect their sin.

Both ideas fit the chapter. The farmer's parable that follows adds a third: God's judgment is not random or unlimited. The threshing does not go on forever, and its aim is to bring out the grain, not to destroy it.

questions: Jerusalem's leaders trusted a political deal they called security. What are the equivalent refuges people rely on today, and how do they fail?
The scoffers dismissed Isaiah's message as childish. What makes people resist simple, clear truth?
The farmer's parable says God knows how much threshing each crop needs. How might that shape the way someone endures a hard season?
